> Hi Nimble folks,
> I am trying to fit a relatively (at least conceptually) straight forward extension to an N-mixture model, where individuals belong to two fully observable groups and groups have different detection probabilities. Total abundance N follows a Poisson distribution and abundance in each group (N.b) is then a multinomial random variable with sample size = N. Here is a model code snippet:
>
> #abundance model
> for (i in 1:nsites){
>     lambda[i]<-exp(alpha + beta*hab[i]) #expected total abundance
>     N[i]~dpois(lambda[i])                        ##total abundance
>     N.b[i,1:2]~dmulti(bprob[1:2], N[i])     ##abundance in each of the two groups
>   }
>
>   #observation model
>   for (j in 1:nsites){
>     for (k in 1:K){
>       for (i in 1:2){                              #loop over two groups of individuals
>         Y[j,k,i]~dbin(dprob[i], N.b[j,i])  #dprob = detection probability for a given group; Y[i,j,k] are repeated counts in each group
>       }}}
>
> The model runs fine in Nimble (JAGS cannot handle the random sample size in the multinomial distribution), but N is not updated - it just sits at the initial value. Any ideas why that might happen? I checked and it is assigned a slice sampler; any reason a different sampler might do the trick?

>

Hi Daniel,
based on some off-list input from Perry, I have re-written the model, but am still having the same issue with N not being updated.
I have copy-pasted code for data generation and the model code below.

###simulate N-mixture data for 2 types of behavior

#set parameters
bprob<-c(0.8, 0.2) #proportion of the population in each behavior category
behav<-length(bprob)
nsites<-50
hab<-sample(c(1,2),nsites, replace = T)-1
alpha<-log(10) ##abundance intercept
beta<-.8 ##effect of hab on abundance
K<-5 #visits
dprob<-c(.5,.9) #detection prob for each behavior category

###create expected and realized abundances
lambda<-exp(alpha+beta*hab)
N<-rpois(nsites, lambda)

### separate out individuals by behavior (site-by-behavior matrix)
Nb<-matrix(rep(NA,behav*nsites),nrow=behav)
for(i in 1:nsites){
  Nb[,i]<-rmultinom(1, N[i], bprob)
}

Nb<-t(Nb)

###create observation data
obs<-array(NA, c(nsites, K, behav))

for (j in 1:nsites){
  for (k in 1:K){

    for (i in 1:behav){
      obs[j,k,i]<-rbinom(1, Nb[j,i],dprob[i])
    }}}

##add unobserved (NA) to obs
obs.u<-array(NA, c(nsites, K, behav+1))
obs.u[1:nsites, 1:K, 1:behav]<-obs

data<-list(Y=obs.u, hab=hab, ones=rep(1, behav))
consts<-list(K=K, behav=behav,nsites=nsites)

## add 1 unobserved as an init
tobs<-apply(obs,1:2,sum) #total observed for each occasion
N.in<-apply(tobs,1, max)+1 #N is max plus 1

#now need inits for unobserved that match N
NbyK<-matrix(N.in, nsites, K)
unobs<-NbyK-tobs
obs.in <http://obs.in><-array(NA, c(nsites, K, behav+1))
obs.in <http://obs.in>[1:nsites, 1:K, 3]<-unobs

pi.in <http://pi.in><-c(apply(obs, 3, sum, na.rm=T)/sum(obs, na.rm = T))

inits<-function(){list(alpha=runif(1), beta=runif(1),
                      dprob=c(0.5, 0.5), bprob=pi.in <http://pi.in>, N=N.in, Y=obs.in <http://obs.in>)}
#
Nbc <- nimbleCode({ ##code into nimble code object
  # Priors
  beta ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
  alpha ~ dnorm(0,0.001)
  #detection

  for (i in 1:2){

    dprob[i] ~ dbeta(1,1)}

  #behavior
  bprob[1:2] ~ ddirch(ones[1:2])

  # Likelihood, abundance

  for (i in 1:nsites){
    lambda[i]<-exp(alpha + beta*hab[i])

    N[i]~dpois(lambda[i])

    #N.b[i,1:2]~dmulti(bprob[1:2], N[i])
  }

  #model for multinomial cell probabilities
  cprob[1]<-bprob[1]*dprob[1] #in category 1 and detected
  cprob[2]<-bprob[2]*dprob[2] #in category 2 and detected
  cprob[3]<-bprob[1]*(1-dprob[1])+bprob[2]*(1-dprob[2]) #not detected

  #observation model
  for (j in 1:nsites){
    for (k in 1:K){

        Y[j,k,1:3]~dmulti(cprob[1:3], N[j])
      }}

  Ntotal<-sum(N[1:nsites])
})

Model <- nimbleModel(Nbc,
                     data=data,#not necessary at this step
                     constants = consts,
                     inits = inits())
NMCMC <- configureMCMC(Model,monitors=c("N","dprob", "bprob"))
NMCMC <- buildMCMC(NMCMC)

CNModel <- compileNimble(Model)
CNMCMC <- compileNimble(NMCMC, project =CNModel)

samples <- runMCMC(CNMCMC, niter = 10000, nburnin = 5000,nchains=1,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)
summ<-summary(samples)

messages.body_plain:
Ok, sounds like you're off and running.

Just in case, or for future reference, here is an idea.

Let's say we have something like the following:

N[i] is number of individuals at site i.
Nobs[i, j, 1:2]  is number of individuals observed in each of states 1 and 2 during visit j to site i.
We assume there are some unobserved individuals during visit j to site i, namely N[i] - sum(Nobs[i, j, 1:2]) unobserved individuals.
We make an N-mixture assumption that N[i] ~ dpois(lambda)
We have multiple sites and multiple visits per site.

So we would want a likelihood contribution from assuming that
[Nobs[i, j, 1:2], N[i] - sum(Nobs[i, j, 1:2])] are multinomial with probabilities prob[1:3] and size N[i].  Here prob[3] is the probability of being unobserved.

The difficulty is that N[i] - sum(Nobs[i, j, 1:2]) is a deterministic calculation, and we can't make a deterministic node also be part of a stochastic declaration.  We could however do the following:

Nobs[i, j, 1:2] ~ dCustomMulti(prob[1:3], N[i])

and write dCustomMulti to internally calculate N[i] - sum(Nobs[i, j, 1:2]) and return the log probability of the desired 3-category multinomial.

I hope it makes some sense.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Great to see this solution.

I'd like to pull together suggestions for OS-specific configuration problems.  Windows problems seem to be most common, and unfortunately we (nimble development team) have limited Windows expertise.  Here are cases / suggestions I've seen.  If we can refine these points, we could put the in the user manual and the web site.

Windows:
1. Be sure to check box to set PATH when installing Rtools.exe.  Atlernatively, set PATH manually using Diba's tip.
2. Be sure Rtools.exe version matches R version.
3. We have seen some problems resolved by re-installing Rtools followed by re-installing nimble.
4. Sometimes R might need to be run as administrator to have appropriate permissions.  (Does anyone have any insight into when this is relevant for nimble?)
5. If there are filesystem or permissions issues, it is possible to install nimble in a local directory.
6. At some point in the past, Windows users reported problems if their file system involved a space in a directory name in the path to RHOME.  I think we have this resolved, so we would be interested if anyone has experience on this.
7. At some point in the past, perhaps for same reason as #6, Windows users reported problems if R is installed on a network drive.  Does anyone have recent experience with this?
8. If problems arise from generating and compiling C++ files in R's tempdir(), one can use the dirName argument to compileNimble to put such files elsewhere, such as in a local work directory.  I think this shouldn't be necessary since tempdir() should be somewhere with write permission, but does anyone know more about this on Windows?

OS X:
1. Newly installed Xcode or command line tools may need to be started once manually to provide a one-time permission before they will work from nimble.
2. If multiple C++ compilers are present on a system, be sure the PATH will find the right one.

Does anyone have any refinements or additions?

Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,

I am just getting into using nimble so forgive me if this has an obvious answer. I am using nimble to run open population spatial capture recapture models and I am struggling with setting up the samplers for stochastic nodes. My model consists of 4 years of data where individual animal activity centers are designated within a discrete statespace. When I use configureMCMC() it defaults to assigning a different sampler to year 1 (posterior predictive) than for years 2-4 (RW) for the stochastic node that assigns these activity centers. All the other node samplers are correct. What is the best way to do this?

I tried using the code outlined on the help page for samplerAssignmentRules function and addRule, but R does not recognize the function.
my_rules <- samplerAssignmentRules(empty = TRUE)
Error in samplerAssignmentRules(empty = TRUE) :
  could not find function "samplerAssignmentRules"

I also looked at the nimbleOptions and it gave me this for the sampler assignment rules section:
$MCMCdefaultSamplerAssignmentRules
[[1]]
Error in cat(x, ..., sep = sep) :
  argument 1 (type 'S4') cannot be handled by 'cat'

I appreciate any guidance on this!
Best
Colby

messages.body_plain:
Colby, thanks so much for your use of NIMBLE, and also posting this question to our list.

The short answer is that the samplerAssignmentRules is a slick way of setting "new rules" for how NIMBLE assigns its default samplers (to the different nodes / dimensions of your model).  That said, for a more practical approach, I'm going to recommend you simply modify the samplers yourself, using the methods of the MCMC configuration (conf) object.  This will be more straightforward and transparent.  e.g.,

## create conf object, and see the default sampler assignments
conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, print = TRUE)

## remove all samplers acting on any component of "sxy" variable
conf$removeSamplers("sxy")

## add a specific type of sampler (say "RW") to all nodes in nodeNames vector
for(n in nodeNames) {
    conf$addSampler(type = "RW", target = n)
}

The process for creating the nodeNames vector can be automated, as well.  We can help with that, if you're able to share more details of your model (either on, or off-list).

And, if your animal activity centers are restricted on a discrete statespace, as you mentioned, then RW Metropolis-Hastings samplers might not be the right choice - in fact, they wouldn't work.  But perhaps I'm not understanding the model setup.

And finally, if the MCMC is assigning posterior_predictive samplers to any set of nodes, then it's because they have no (stochastic) dependencies, and that is, in fact, the best choice sampler for them.  Is there any chance the model definition isn't quite right?  I'm just guessing, though, it's hard to say without seeing the model.

Cheers!  Happy Friday!

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Good questions all around, Colby.  And it sounds like an interesting ecological problem you have.

Short answer, either way you have it would work, technically.  But by nature of how the sampling would work in the first dunif parameterization (activ.s[i,t] ~ dunif(1,  nPix)), I think in practice it would fail pretty hard, since M-H sampling will generally work better with "well-behaved" distributions, eg. ideally unimodal, whereas here, since the probabilities you describe in s.probs could induce any such posterior over this space, I think you're better with the second option you gave, the dcat parameterization.  (even the first way, without using s.probs and using the uniform distribution, I suppose it would work fine, but still feels less natural to me).  So I'm going to suggest the second, but encourage you to try both, and compare results.

On another note, I'll recommend you use conf$printSamplers(), rather than conf$getSamplers().  The getSamplers() method has an important place sometimes, but it's intended more for *programatic* manipulation of the conf object.  It's main role is to *return* a list with all the configuration information - not to print that information nicely for you, which is the primary function of printSamplers.

Finally, as for your questions about how to assign / remove samplers, just take a look at the short example I put together, below.  Hopefully it will answer your questions.

Hope this helps!  Keep in touch!  Thanks for using NIMBLE.

library(nimble)

code <- nimbleCode({

    for(i in 1:M) {
        for(t in 1:Year) {

            ##activ.s[i,t] ~ dunif(1,  nPix)
            ##s.x[i,t] <-  myCalculation(Mask[,2],round(activ.s[i,t]))
            ##s.y[i,t] <-  myCalculation(Mask[,3],round(activ.s[i,t]))

            activ.s[i,t] ~ dcat(s.probs[1:nPix])

            s[i,t,1] <- myCalculation(Mask[,2], activ.s[i,t])

            s[i,t,2] <- myCalculation(Mask[,3], activ.s[i,t])
        }
    }

})

myCalculation <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(grid = double(1), index = double()) {

    return(grid[index])
    returnType(double(0))
})

M <- 180
Year <- 4
nPix <- 1000
s.probs <- rep(1/nPix, nPix)   ## uniform probabilities
Mask <- array(0, c(nPix, 3))   ## I know that 0's don't make sense here

constants <- list(M=M, Year=Year, nPix=nPix, s.probs=s.probs, Mask=Mask)

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants)  ## you probably want data and inits also

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)

conf$printSamplers()

## if you see posterior_predictive samplers assigned,
## again it's because nothing in your model (in particular:
## no latent states, nor any data) *depend* on those
## nodes.  So the MCMC simply takes draws from their
## prior distribution to sample them, because in that
## case, prior = posterior.

## Anyway, let's remove whatever samplers were assigned,
## and I'd recommend either 'categorial' samplers,
## which could be slow but will sample well, or 'slice' samplers

## In response to this question:
## How do I keep this format when changing just the nodes activ.s[i,1] to a different sampler?
sNodes <- Rmodel$expandNodeNames(paste0('activ.s[1:',M,',1]'))
conf$removeSamplers(sNodes)

## this next scalarComponents = TRUE is a very new feature,
## just added within the past month or so.  tbh I'm not
## sure if it made the most recent release or not (?)
## so let me know if it doesn't work:
conf$addSampler(target = sNodes, type = 'slice', scalarComponents = TRUE)

## to change samplers on *all* the 'activ.s' nodes,
## say to the other option of categorical samplers:
sNodesAll <- Rmodel$expandNodeNames('activ.s')
conf$removeSamplers(sNodesAll)
conf$addSampler(target = sNodesAll, type = 'categorical', scalarComponents = TRUE)

Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)
... compile, run, etc....

Gregory, thanks for your email, and your use of NIMBLE.  If I'm not mistaken, your code is nearly spot-on for doing this (with a single ragged array structure).  Slightly modified code appears below.  The only minor disadvantage I can imagine here, is that the ragged array structure will result in the allocation of some unnecessary memory (specifically: the unused elements of those "rows" aside from the row of complete length.  If this memory is a legitimate concern, then we could discuss other approaches.

Anyway, this runs fine for me, and hopefully answers your question:

library(nimble)

m <- 5
ns <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 3)       ## number of elements in each of the 'm' groups

poisCode <- nimbleCode({
    ##
    ## Parameters with priors
    for (cell in 1:m) {
        lambda[cell] ~ dunif(0, 5000)
    }
    ##
    ## The data and its probability distributions
    for (cell in 1:m) {
        for (sample in 1:ns[cell]) {   ## changed index to 'cell', rather than 'm'
            x[sample, cell] ~ dpois(lambda = lambda[cell])
        }
    }
})

x <- array(0, c(max(ns), m))   ## your actual data here

constants <- list(m = m, ns = ns)
data <- list(x = x)
inits <- list(lambda = rep(1, m))

Rmodel <- nimbleModel(poisCode, constants, data, inits)

Rmodel$calculate()
## -81.58597   ## looks good, model is fully initialized

messages.body_plain:
Yes, it appears there's some confusion about the nimbleMCMC() function, which you said you're using, versus nimbleModel(), which the code you provided uses.

nimbleModel: creates and uncompiled "Rmodel" object, which can later be used to configure and build and MCMC.  This function takes only *one list containing one set of initial values*.  Not a list of lists of initial values.

nimbleMCMC: can take an inits function, and a single list of initial values, or a list of lists of initial values (as you're trying to do, one for each chain).  Then it builds, compiles, and runs the MCMC.

Correct usage examples of both are shown below.  Note that the nimbleModel() function takes initsList[[1]], that is, only the first element of initsList, as the "inits" argument:

library(nimble)

nCode <- nimbleCode({
    b1 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    k ~ dnorm(0, 1)
})

initsList <- list(
    list(b1 = 0.7, k=1),
    list(b1 = 0.8, k=1),
    list(b1 = 0.9, k=1),
    list(b1 = 1.0, k=1)
)

## run 4 chains of MCMC:
samplesList <- nimbleMCMC(
    code = nCode,
    constants = list(),
    data = list(),

    inits = initsList,
    nchains = 4
)

## construct an uncompiled nimble model object:
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(
    code = nCode,
    constants = list(),
    data = list(),
    inits = initsList[[1]]   ## note the change here.
)
